title: Nasdaq Tumbles 2.6% as Oil Surge and AI Spending Fears Hit Stocks
excerpt: The Nasdaq suffered its worst day since June as Brent topped $113, Meta slid on AI costs, and investors fled to Treasuries.
body:
• The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.6% to 26,008.86 on October 22, its steepest drop since June, while the S&P 500 fell 1.21% to 7,663.43.
  • Meta fell about 6-7% despite beating revenue expectations, as investors focused on rising AI spending, a first cash outflow in more than a decade, and plans for non-voting shares.
  • Brent crude settled up 3% at $113.03 a barrel and WTI at $99.27, a five-month high, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia and reports of possible renewed US-Israel strikes on Iran.
  • For portfolio holders, the 10-year Treasury yield fell 17 basis points to 4.974% as money moved to safety — a sign the selloff was about risk, not just earnings.

US stocks fell sharply on Thursday as a surge in oil prices revived inflation fears and a fresh wave of concern about artificial intelligence spending hit technology shares. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.60% to 26,008.86, its steepest daily decline since June, while the S&P 500 fell 1.21% to 7,663.43, its worst session since July, according to Invezz. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.02% to 52,867.98.

The intraday picture was similar earlier in the session. Moneycontrol, via Bloomberg, put the Nasdaq 100 down 2.2% at midday in New York, with Meta down 6.2% at that point. By the close, the losses had broadened across chips and AI infrastructure names.

Tech led the decline

Meta Platforms fell around 7% despite reporting better-than-expected third-quarter revenue and an upbeat outlook. Investors focused instead on rising AI expenditure, its first cash outflow in more than a decade, and plans to issue non-voting shares to fund expansion. Earlier, Reuters reported Meta slipped in premarket trading after introducing the new shares, reviving scrutiny of the capital needed to stay competitive in AI.

Chipmakers sold off with it. Advanced Micro Devices fell more than 8%, Micron Technology declined 6% and Nvidia lost 4%. CoreWeave, a provider of AI-focused cloud infrastructure, dropped more than 10% on debt and financing concerns. Tesla also declined despite reporting positive free cash flow and lowering its 2026 capital expenditure plans. In premarket trading Reuters had Tesla down 5.3% after the capex cut raised questions about the pace of its AI and robotics expansion, with Intel down 5.1% and other chip names down 2.9-5.3%.

"Concerns about the sustainability of AI spending hurt markets and rising oil prices stoked concerns about the threat posed by inflation."

— Russ Mould, Investment Director, AJ Bell

Oil at a five-month high

Brent crude futures rose 3% to settle at $113.03 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate advanced 2.18% to $99.27. Reuters put Brent up more than 3% to about $112 in early trading after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked fears of supply disruption and a wider Middle East conflict.

Invezz reported the move followed reports that the US and Israel were considering renewed strikes against Iran after next month's US midterm elections, alongside the Houthi attacks on Saudi targets. Higher energy prices pushed up inflation expectations at a moment when US jobless claims remained near multi-decade lows, leaving the Federal Reserve little room to look past price pressure. Markets were pricing in the possibility of another 25-basis-point rate increase before year-end, according to Invezz.

Bonds rallied as stocks fell

Treasury yields fell as investors sought safety. The benchmark 10-year yield fell more than 17 basis points to 4.974%, its lowest in almost a month, and the two-year yield dropped more than 16 basis points to 4.66%. That flight to safety contrasted with the inflation impulse from oil — investors were buying duration on growth and financing worries even as energy pushed the other way. Bitcoin fell 3.4% in early trading, Reuters reported, in a broader risk-off move.

Earnings outside technology were mixed rather than uniformly weak. Of 111 S&P 500 companies that had reported, 83% had beaten analyst expectations, according to LSEG data cited by Invezz. Procter & Gamble rose after beating revenue estimates despite warning on commodity costs, Lockheed Martin gained after raising its sales and profit forecasts, and Spotify advanced on a stronger fourth-quarter profit outlook.

What comes next

The next test is whether oil holds above $110 and whether upcoming mega-cap earnings give investors a clearer payback timeline for AI capital spending. If Brent stays elevated, inflation expectations and Fed pricing will stay under pressure. If AI spending guidance stabilises, Thursday's move could prove a sharp repricing rather than the start of a longer drawdown — but the semiconductor index has now extended losses from its June record high, and investors are demanding proof, not promises, on returns.
